title: Assessing the Added Value of Earth Observations for Multi‐Model Kilometer‐Scale Hydrological Modeling Across Contrasting Basins
content:
Abstract

Earth observation (EO) products provide spatially and temporally detailed information on key water-cycle processes, yet their value for improving hydrological and land-surface model simulations remains uncertain. Here, we evaluate high-resolution EO data for daily streamflow simulations at ≈ ${\approx} $1 km resolution across contrasting hydroclimatic and data-density regimes in Europe and Africa, using up to five model structures (five in the Po, four in the Rhine and three in the Tugela). We explore two complementary pathways: (a) replacing conventional meteorological forcing with EO-based precipitation, and (b) estimating model parameters with EO constraints on soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and snow cover, either alone or jointly with streamflow. Model skill is quantified using the Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and its components, based on paired gauge comparisons. Results show that EO precipitation forcing improves streamflow simulations in the Po and Tugela river basins, but reduces skill in the Rhine. Calibration against EO variables alone yields mixed outcomes, whereas joint calibration with EO variables and streamflow, available for three of the models, gives more consistent improvements, particularly for TETIS in the Tugela and mHM in the Po. KGE decomposition reveals that improved variability alignment is the dominant contributor to these gains, with changes in bias and timing playing secondary roles. Despite differences across models and basins, our findings show that EO integration can enhance kilometer-scale hydrological simulations in specific model–basin configurations, particularly when combined with discharge information. This highlights both the potential and the current limits of available EO products as complementary constraints for operational hydrology, flood and drought early warning, and climate-resilient water management.
